look_here_first: Start with the fruiting branch. Western soapberry has alternate pinnately compound leaves with strongly asymmetric leaflets and clusters of round translucent amber-yellow drupes that often persist into winter. Then confirm the small cream flowers and floral disk.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: deciduous small tree, often clonal and thicket-forming

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: leaves alternate, once-pinnately compound, without stipules

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: leaflets usually numerous and conspicuously asymmetric at the base

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: small cream to whitish flowers in branched terminal clusters

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: floral disk present around the superior ovary

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: round fleshy one-seeded drupes ripening yellow to amber and becoming translucent

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: fruit clusters often persist after leaf fall

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Alternate pinnate leaves usually carry many asymmetrical lanceolate leaflets; the missing terminal leaflet and unequal leaflet bases are useful field cues.

key_traits.label: Flower
key_traits.text: Small pale flowers occur in branched clusters. A floral disk is part of the Sapindaceae reproductive plan.

key_traits.label: Fruit
key_traits.text: Round one-seeded drupes become yellow to amber and translucent; the saponin-rich pericarp gives the tree its soapberry name.

key_traits.label: Field tip
key_traits.text: Without fruit, compare the alternate pinnate leaves carefully against Rhus and Pistacia. With fruit, the translucent soapberry drupes are highly distinctive.
